🥧 It's Thanksgiving Eve! Happy cooking and safe travels. Smart Brevity™ count: 1,377 words ... 5 mins. Thanks to Noah Bressner for orchestrating. Edited by Bill Kole.

🗳️ House Democrats added one more to their incoming majority, the biggest sweep since 1990. The chamber now stands at 259-173, with three races undecided. Democrats have gained 45 House seats so far. Go deeper.

💰 Trump Accounts crossed the $1 billion mark in donations from friends and family.
 
 
1 big thing: AI's free-will fight
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Top AI executives are increasingly pushing back against a common view inside Anthropic: that humanity should surrender decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, sources told Axios' Madison Mills.

  • Some Silicon Valley insiders see that as a first step toward giving up our free will.

Why it matters: The debate has picked up steam as top AI companies develop models many employees consider too powerful to ever release.

The critics haven't named Anthropic, but their calls to keep humans in charge run counter to a view some in Silicon Valley associate with its CEO, Dario Amodei.

  • Amodei has repeatedly said it would be preferable to turn over decision-making for "life-critical" cases to AI when systems far surpass human intelligence. He's also said AI should oversee research and potentially distribute economic resources.

Flashback: A product vision slide from several years ago that was revealed during litigation described Anthropic's "vision for a better world" as a "utopia ruled by god in a box."

🖼️ The big picture: The thinking for Amodei and others is that once AI can demonstrably cure diseases, safeguard humans from harming themselves or prevent disasters better than any person, refusing to hand over control becomes irrational — or even unethical.

  • Proponents point to self-driving cars to make their case: Once statistical evidence points to autonomous vehicles being safer than human drivers, it is logical for humans to drive far less, if at all, they say.
  • Inside Anthropic, a consensus has developed that humanity will — and in many cases should — safely hand over authority to superintelligent systems rather than fighting to retain control, according to people familiar with internal discussions.
  • An Anthropic spokesperson said Amodei has advocated for human control of AI in public remarks and has developed the technology to ensure Claude doesn't undermine human oversight.

Friction point: Two of the industry's most prominent executives say people should keep the final say, even if AI can outthink them.

  • Meta's top AI leader, Alexandr Wang, wrote on X that "we should not be okay with a 'handover' of society to AI."
  • OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said earlier this month: "I want people to have the agency over the future. ... I think it's really important that we advocate for this."

2. 🦠 COVID rises on brink of holidays
 
Recreated from Pandemic Mitigation Collaborative. Map: Axios

There's a lot of COVID going around, and acute respiratory illness is on the rise heading into Thanksgiving, Axios' Caitlin Owens writes.

  • Why it matters: The pandemic's crisis phase is long behind us. But it's still not holiday fun to catch COVID.

🧮 By the numbers: The Pandemic Mitigation Collaborative, a Tulane University project, estimates 1.4 million new daily infections, the highest level in 14+ months.

  • Flu infections are also rising in 34 states. RSV cases are increasing in 39.

3. 🎤 "The Axios Show": Wes Moore on "AI earthquake"
 
Mike Allen interviews Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) in the Maryland State House in Annapolis on Monday. Photo: JaMar Jones for Axios

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), a potential 2028 presidential contender, told me on "The Axios Show" that Washington is leaving Americans vulnerable to AI because of billionaire greed and clout.

  • Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, said that after an "AI earthquake" helped propel Democrats to huge midterm gains, Congress must treat oversight of the technology as an "emergency" for the first 100 hours of Democratic control.

Why it matters: Moore, 48, focused on AI early, with an executive order in 2024. He has used his NGA leadership roles to work across the aisle on AI protections, arguing that Marylanders can't afford to wait for Washington and shouldn't have to wait for a disaster.

The governor's key points:

  • On the pace of regulation: "We are watching a fast-moving technology that is being protected at a snail's pace."
  • On why people hate AI: "Genesis 1 talks about how God gave humanity dominion over all land, air and sea. And that dominion was given to humanity, not to robots."
  • On a bubble: "We are in a bubble because you cannot have that much influence by such a small group of companies."

4. ✈️ Scoop: Thanksgiving flight boom
 
Data: FAA. (The numbers cover the Monday before Thanksgiving through the Tuesday after. The data includes flights tracked by air traffic control under instrument flight rules.) Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios

Thanksgiving week air travel is expected to reach a 16-year high, with 417,775 flights forecast over the nine-day holiday period from Nov. 23 through Dec. 1, Axios' Alex Isenstadt writes from FAA figures.

  • Why it matters: The Thanksgiving rush will test the Trump administration's push to improve reliability and minimize flight delays and cancellations after the historic ground stop earlier this month.

👀 Behind the scenes: A newly assembled "tiger team" tasked with improving the air traffic control system's reliability has been meeting daily for the past week, a White House official told Axios.

5. 🎯 Scoop: Midterm friendly fire
 

Photo illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Photos: Andrew Harnik, Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images
 

A top executive at one of the Republican Party's most influential consulting firms was involved in a multimillion-dollar effort to defeat two GOP senators — Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska — in midterms, Axios' Alex Isenstadt has learned.

  • The firm, Axiom Strategies, is widely seen as the GOP's biggest consulting operation, with deep ties to Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and other prominent Republican figures.

Why it matters: It's exceedingly rare — if not unprecedented — for an executive at a major political consulting firm to work for groups seeking to defeat senators from the firm's own party in a general election.

🔎 Zoom in: Federal election records identify Thomas Datwyler, who was listed on Axiom's website as CEO of its AxCapital division, as treasurer and custodian of records for three super PACs that reported more than $9.9 million in spending that targeted Husted and Sullivan, who lost their reelection bids.

  • Axiom founder Jeff Roe learned of Datwyler's involvement from a lawyer on Oct. 30 and demanded his resignation, according to a source with knowledge of the situation.
  • Datwyler resigned that day, and Axiom says it will finish unwinding its relationship with him by Dec. 31. People familiar with his work said he sometimes accepted clients without scrutinizing their objectives.
  • Roe contacted the White House to inform officials of what he had discovered, the source said.

6. ⚖️ Trump faces wave of ICE lawsuits
 
White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller walks into the briefing room before President Trump's press conference last week. Photo: Alex Brandon/AP

The Trump administration is facing the first of possibly hundreds of lawsuits testing whether it can be held liable for how immigration officers acted during the ICE crackdowns, Axios' Brittany Gibson writes.

  • Why it matters: These cases could force the administration to defend the conduct of officers operating under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and now-retired Border Patrol Commander-at-large Greg Bovino.

Democracy Forward, an advocacy litigation nonprofit, filed its first Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) case on Monday on behalf of Dayanne Figueroa.

  • Figueroa, a U.S. citizen, was arrested during Operation Midway Blitz in Chicago in October 2025.
  • Video footage of Figueroa's arrest, after dropping her son off at school, shows officers driving into her vehicle and dragging her out of her car by her legs in a chaotic scene with multiple witnesses.

Go deeper: Exclusive interview with Figueroa.
 
 
7. 🏛️ Incoming Dem chairs have lots of Nvidia Qs
 
Employees applaud as Jensen Huang returns Monday to Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif. Screengrab from social-media video: Zhengzhong Tu via Reuters

The incoming chairs of the Senate Foreign Relations, Banking, Finance, Armed Services and Commerce committees said last night that they'll probe these questions about Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang:

  1. "Which administration officials engaged Nvidia or its board about Huang's return, and what assurances or commitments did they give?"
  2. "What intelligence assessments informed that advocacy [and] which national security agencies were consulted?"
  3. "When did the president, the vice president, and other senior officials first learn of Huang's relationship and the associated counterintelligence or national security concerns, and what actions did they take?"
  • Read the statement.
 
 
8. 🏈 NFL takes over Thanksgiving week
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios
 

The NFL is taking over Thanksgiving week, with a first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game tonight that includes a halftime performance and an expanded partnership with Netflix, Axios Media Trends author Sara Fischer writes.

  • It's part of a broader effort by the league to capitalize on holidays, when families are more likely to spend time watching TV together.

Netflix's deal gives it the rights to the pre-Turkey Day game through 2029, starting with tonight's Packers-Rams matchup. U2 will perform at halftime.
